# The Library of Unfinished Things

There is, I think, a secret library in every city.

It does not occupy a recognizable building. It has no marble stairs, no return desk, no brass lamps glowing under green shades. You cannot find it on a map, though pieces of it are everywhere: in apartment closets, in garage corners, in cloud-storage folders, in the backs of notebooks, in cabinets full of cables whose purposes nobody remembers. Its collection consists entirely of unfinished things.

There are half-written novels in this library, of course. They sit in long rows, their first chapters polished by hope and their later pages dissolving into notes such as “research this,” “make ending better,” and “maybe this character is actually the sister?” There are paintings stopped at the awkward stage where the sky is blue but somehow dead, where the foreground is only a promise in pencil. There are languages learned halfway: lists of verbs, tiny victories in pronunciation, notebooks filled with sentences about train stations and ordering coffee.

There are sourdough starters abandoned in refrigerators. Exercise plans begun on Mondays. Guitar chords printed from the internet. Business ideas drafted late at night. Email replies saved as drafts because the right tone could not be found. Family histories researched until one confusing census record made the whole past feel inaccessible. Gardens designed but never planted. Gardens planted but never weeded. Gardens weeded faithfully until August, when the heat became personal.

The library is enormous.

Most people assume unfinished things are failures. They look at the novel with fifty pages and think: not a novel. They look at the running shoes used for three mornings and think: not a runner. They look at a box of watercolor supplies and think: wasted money. But the secret library does not organize its books according to success or failure. It is older, stranger, and kinder than that. It understands that a human life is not a factory line for completed objects. It is a weather system. Plans form, gather force, drift, collide, and sometimes vanish before reaching the ground.

The unfinished thing is not always evidence of weakness. Sometimes it is evidence that a person had enough imagination to begin.

Beginnings are acts of optimism, even when they arrive disguised as frustration. A person who starts learning to cook may be tired of eating takeout, but underneath that annoyance is a belief that dinner could be different. A person who buys seeds in March is making a small treaty with the future. A person who opens a blank document to write a story is saying, however quietly, that something invisible might be made visible through effort.

This is no small thing.

We tend to praise completion because completion is easy to display. You can hold up the diploma, publish the book, hang the painting, post the before-and-after photographs. Completion makes a satisfying shape. It has edges. It permits congratulations. But beginnings and middle stages are often less presentable. They are full of uncertainty, contradictions, detours, embarrassment, and the daily humbling fact that wanting to do something is not the same as knowing how.

The middle is where most of life happens.

A child is praised for taking first steps and celebrated for eventually walking, but nobody applauds the years in between, when walking is simply walking. The same is true of almost everything else. The dramatic moments make the story: the decision to move to a new city, the wedding, the resignation letter, the first day of school, the final performance. Yet a life is built mostly from the unphotographed middle: washing dishes, taking buses, replying to messages, standing in grocery store aisles, becoming gradually better or worse at something without noticing.

Perhaps that is why unfinished projects make us uneasy. They remind us of the middle. They reveal that we are not entirely the heroes of our own narratives. We do not move cleanly from desire to achievement. We wander. We forget. We get tired. We become interested in something else. We discover that the dream looked better from a distance. We discover, sometimes mercifully, that the dream was never really ours.

There are projects we abandon because we are afraid. These deserve tenderness, but also examination. Fear is a skilled archivist. It preserves every bad review, every awkward conversation, every early failure, every time someone laughed at an idea before it had become strong enough to defend itself. Fear can make a person confuse hesitation with wisdom. It can persuade us that waiting until we are more talented, more confident, more prepared, more certain is a form of responsibility.

Often it is only delay.

But there are also projects we abandon because we have learned something. Not every path deserves loyalty. A person may quit law school and become a carpenter, stop performing music and become a better listener, leave a prestigious job and recover an ordinary morning. From the outside, this can look like failure. From the inside, it may be the first honest decision in years.

The secret library knows the difference, though it does not judge either one harshly. It has shelves for fear and shelves for wisdom. Sometimes the same manuscript appears in both sections.

I like to imagine the librarians there: patient, dust-covered figures with ink-stained fingers and no interest in productivity systems. They do not scold anyone for overdue books, because every book in their care is overdue by definition. Instead, they preserve the evidence of attempted lives. They keep the sketches, the notebooks, the recipes with ingredients crossed out, the maps with routes only partly traveled.

Perhaps they occasionally take a volume from the shelf and place it somewhere more visible.

A person might be cleaning out a drawer after ten years and find a folder labeled “photography.” Inside are notes from a class they barely remember taking, along with a few printed pictures: a friend’s face in afternoon light, rain on a window, an old man feeding pigeons in a square. The person pauses. Not because the photographs are brilliant, necessarily, but because they contain an earlier self, someone who noticed things. And perhaps that self is not gone. Perhaps it has been waiting quietly in the library.

This is one of the strange gifts of unfinished things: they can remain alive.

A completed project often closes a door. The final draft is submitted. The house is sold. The last performance ends. The thing enters the world and becomes, to some degree, separate from its maker. An unfinished project remains porous. It can change as we change. It can be returned to under new weather.

The abandoned novel may become a short story. The failed garden may become a balcony full of herbs. The unlearned language may reappear years later when a new neighbor needs help carrying groceries. The old business idea may reveal itself not as a company but as a hobby, a service, a friendship, or a question worth keeping.

Not everything needs to be rescued, of course. Some unfinished things are best left on their shelves. There is dignity in deciding not to finish a task that no longer belongs to you. The trouble is that many people never consciously decide. They carry their abandoned projects as invisible debts. Every unopened box of supplies becomes an accusation. Every unread book becomes proof of intellectual negligence. Every saved article becomes a tiny monument to a life they believe they should be living.

This is exhausting.

It may help to hold an occasional amnesty.

Choose a day and gather the unfinished things around you. Open the drawer. Look through the digital folders. Find the book with the receipt still inside it. Take out the knitting project, the language app, the correspondence course, the journal started during a difficult year. Then ask each one a simple question: Do I still want you?

Not: Should I want you? Not: Would a more disciplined person want you? Not: What would it say about me if I gave you up?

Do I still want you?

The answer may be yes. In that case, begin again, but begin smaller. Do not promise yourself a masterpiece. Promise ten minutes. Promise one page. Promise one seed in a pot, one song practiced badly, one email sent without perfect wording. The smallest sincere action is more powerful than the grandest intention admired from afar.

The answer may be no. In that case, let the thing go. Donate the supplies. Delete the folder. Recycle the notes. Thank the former version of yourself for trying to become someone through that project. Then release them from the job.

People sometimes speak about “becoming the person you want to be,” as if identity were a distant destination reached through relentless self-improvement. But perhaps we are not meant to become one final person. Perhaps we are more like houses with rooms added over time. Some rooms are used constantly; some are locked; some are full of boxes; some are bright only in the morning. There may be a studio you once built for painting, now used for storing winter coats. That does not mean the room was a mistake. It means houses, like people, have histories.

The best homes are not those with no unused corners. They are the ones where the inhabitants can still move freely.

There is a particular sadness in modern life that comes from confusing possibility with obligation. We are told that we can do almost anything if we work hard enough, optimize our schedules, cultivate the right habits, wake up at the right hour, drink the right green substance, read the right books, and refuse distraction with sufficient moral force. The promise is intoxicating. It also contains a trap.

If everything is possible, then every unchosen path feels like a personal failure.

But no life can contain every life. To become a marine biologist is not to become a baker, even if you love bread. To raise children in one country is not to spend your twenties wandering through another. To write a novel may mean not writing a hundred essays. To care deeply for one person may mean missing the chance to know many others. There is no perfect arrangement in which every talent is used, every interest explored, every relationship nourished, every trip taken, every book read, every body kept healthy, every career possibility honored.

The cost of choosing is loss. That is not an error in the system. It is the system.

Maturity may be less about maximizing one’s options than about grieving them properly. Not dramatically, not with bitterness, but with respect. To say: I could have been that person, perhaps. I am not. I will not be. And this life, the one I have, is still here asking to be lived.

The secret library contains many possible selves. The dancer who stopped after an injury. The astronomer who chose nursing school. The chef who became an accountant. The person who almost moved to Lisbon, almost called their father, almost started a community garden, almost learned to swim. These selves are not ghosts that must haunt us. They can be ancestors of the present. They gave us preferences, scars, skills, stories, and a more complicated understanding of what we desire.

Even regret has its uses when it is not allowed to become a permanent residence.

Regret can sharpen attention. It can make us call sooner, apologize sooner, begin sooner. It can teach us that time is not an abstract resource but a material condition of love. We do not have endless opportunities to visit someone, to ask a question, to take a walk at sunset with a person who will one day no longer be there. The knowledge is painful, but it can make ordinary moments luminous.

Perhaps this is why unfinished things matter so much. They are reminders that time is real. Every project requires not just talent or money or courage, but hours. Hours are portions of a life. To spend them is to choose what one will not do instead.

And yet, for all that, we must guard against becoming too solemn about our choices. Not everything needs to justify its existence. Some projects can remain gloriously impractical. Learn a song nobody will hear. Make a chair badly. Write letters you never send. Memorize the names of clouds. Bake a cake shaped like a castle. Study the migration patterns of birds in a park you visit only twice a year.

There is a kind of freedom in doing something without turning it into a credential, a side hustle, a brand, or a proof of worth. The world has enough measurements already. A private pleasure needs no spreadsheet.

Children understand this before adults teach them otherwise. A child drawing with crayons does not usually ask whether the result will advance a long-term strategic goal. The drawing is the goal. The blue horse exists because blue was available and horses are interesting and the page was empty.

Adults are often embarrassed by this kind of purposelessness. We have learned to ask what something is for. But the question can become a locked gate. What is a walk for? What is a poem for? What is the use of staring at the moon from a fire escape, or baking bread for a neighbor, or learning the name of a tree?

Sometimes the answer is simply that life is not a problem to be solved entirely by utility.

The world is full of things that exceed their function. A window is useful because it lets in light, but it also frames clouds. A cup is useful because it holds tea, but it can become a favorite cup because of a chip in its rim, the way its handle fits a hand, the memory of a kitchen where it was first used. A city street carries people from one place to another, but it can also hold a musician’s melody, the smell of rain on pavement, an argument drifting from an open window, the sudden sight of someone you thought you had forgotten.

Meaning arrives sideways.

Perhaps we need unfinished things because they keep us open to that fact. A fully completed, perfectly optimized life would be intolerably narrow. It would have no room for revising a belief, taking an unexpected turn, rediscovering an old interest, or admitting that a plan was wrong. It would be tidy, perhaps, but not alive.

To live well is not to complete every chapter neatly. It is to remain available to revision.

This does not mean drifting without commitment. Commitment is one of the deepest forms of freedom we have. To commit to a craft, a person, a place, a cause, a difficult truth—these choices give shape to the days. But real commitment is not the same as punishing rigidity. It includes returning after absence. It includes changing methods. It includes forgiving the self who could not carry everything at once.

A musician who has not played in years can still touch the instrument again. A friendship that has gone quiet can sometimes be renewed with one honest message. A person who has treated their body carelessly can take one walk today. A writer can write one sentence after a decade of silence.

None of these acts erase the lost time. That is not their purpose.

Their purpose is to make the present less empty.

The library’s greatest secret may be that it is not only a mausoleum for abandoned ambitions. It is also a seed bank. Every unfinished thing contains, at minimum, a record of attention. You cared enough to begin. You saw a possibility. You reached toward it. Even if you did not continue, the reaching changed you.

Some projects teach us how much we do not want something. That is useful knowledge. Some teach us patience. Some reveal an ability we would otherwise never have suspected. Some bring us to people who remain important long after the original project has disappeared. A failed theater audition may lead to a friendship. A botched attempt at pottery may lead to a weekly ritual. A short-lived job may lead to the city where a person eventually feels at home.

We are poor judges of which moments matter while we are living them.

The thread that appears broken may be woven elsewhere.

So perhaps when we encounter the evidence of our unfinished lives, we should resist the urge to sneer. Let us not call ourselves lazy too quickly, or foolish, or incapable. Let us look with curiosity. What did I hope for here? What interrupted me? What did I learn? What still glows, even faintly?

Then, if something glows, protect the ember.

And if nothing does, close the book gently.

Somewhere, in the secret library, a librarian will take it from your hands. They will label it carefully, not “failure,” not “waste,” not “proof that you never had what it takes,” but something more accurate.

They will write:

**An attempt made by a living person, during a particular season, under conditions not fully known.**
